notes.1a: This proved to be the hardest part of Question 1 , with only about one - quarter of candidates getting it correct. M any candidates may not have realise d that the question asked for a compound and selected graphite from the list, rather than silicon( IV ) oxide.
notes.1b: Propane was the most common incorrect answer, with candidates either unclear on the meaning of unsaturated or confusing alkanes with alkenes. Ethanol was also a common incorrect answer, with many not realis ing that it is not a hydrocarbon.
notes.1c: This was challenging to many candidates and silicon( IV ) oxide and calcium oxide were common incorrect answers.
notes.1e: There was evidence of alkanes being confused with alkenes by some candidates as propane was the most common incorrect answer.
notes.1f: Two answers were required and silicon( IV ) oxide was correctly chosen far more frequently than calcium oxide. Oxygen was often paired with silicon( IV ) oxide.
notes.1g: Most candidates recognised that an organic molecule was required but propene and ethanol were common incorrect answers.
notes.1h: This question was generally well answered although the other organic molecules propane and propene were commonly chosen.
notes.1hi: This was well answered with oxygen being the only common incorrect answer.
notes.2a: Both protons and neutrons were required but a common error was to give only one of the particles.
notes.2bi: Candidates usually performed well on this question. The majority were able to give the correct numbers of electrons, neutrons and protons for the sulfur atom. However, many were unable to link the charge on the sulfide ion with the correct number of elect rons, and the number was often given as 16 rather than 18. Sometimes the neutron column was seen as 34 and 32.
notes.2bii: Some candidates did not attempt the question or found it very challenging and did not seem to know that isotopic mass  abundance was required for both isotopes . Candidates should be encouraged to show all their working and not to just write their final calculated answer due to the possibility of errors being made and thus no credit being gained for the use of a correct method. The most common errors seen were: averaging of the two relative masses 32 and 34 to gain 33 without using the percentage abundances; answers of 32 seen without working out (perhaps using the mass number of sulfur given in the Periodic Table); correctly ca lculated answers of 32.1 that were then incorrectly rounded to a final answer of 32 or 32.0.
notes.2biii: Many candidates had the idea that carbon was required but chose C or just ‘carbon’. Hydrogen and sulfur were also frequently seen incorrect answers.
notes.2c: This proved challenging to many candidates. A wide variety of incorrect answers was seen for both parts. The question asked for a formula for both the atom and ion but this was often ignored and names were given instead. ‘ O ’ was commonly given as the atom. The ion often did not have a + 2+ positive charge or was an element that does not form positive ions, for example F or O .
notes.3ai: Ionic (bonding) was the most common incorrect answer.
notes.3aii: Those candidates that were able to identify metallic bonding in (a)(i) were usually able to correctly name positive ions and electrons, although a common misunderstanding was to give examples of other metals. T hose candidates that incorrectly named ionic bonding in (a)(i) were able to gain credit for naming negative ions as one of the particles but examples of ionic compounds were often given instead of particles.
notes.3aiii: Ions was the only common incorrect answer.
notes.3bi: Although the definition of an alloy is given in the syllabus, this question was often poorly answered. The word ‘mixture’ was often absent and many candidates referred to a compound or a combination of elements. The need for a metal to be present in an alloy was often missing.
notes.3bii: Most candidates knew that copper was the other substance in brass. Common incorrect answers were tin and iron.
notes.3ci: This was poorly answered and only a few candidates achieved both marking points. The question asked for two observations to show that the zinc carbonate was in excess and candidates needed to consider what visible evidence there would be that the acid had been used up and the reaction was over. The only two acceptable observations were : 1 . that the solid would stop dissolving/disappearing and 2 . there would be no more effervescence on addition of more zinc carbonate. ‘ No more gas is produced’ and ‘the reaction stops’ are not observations. A solid seen at the bottom should not be describ ed as a precipitate in this case. Many candidates wrote that there would be bubbling, rather than ‘bubbling would stop’. C andidates who performed less well simply repeated the wording from the question stem about zinc carbonate being in excess, or wrote other excerpts from the method, rather than giving observations.
notes.3cii: T here was confusion for some candidates between the terms filtrate and residue and a very common answer was zinc carbonate. C andidates who performed less well named filter paper or a process such as filtration or evaporation.
notes.3ciii: The expected answers of zinc oxide or zinc hydroxide were commonly seen. However, frequent incorrect answers were zinc nitrate and zinc chloride.
notes.3civ: The definition of s aturated solution is given in the syllabus and many candidates successfully repeated th is . Those who used different terminology often produced incomplete or incorrect statements. There was often confusion between the terms solvent, solute and solution. Some candidates thought that a saturated solution was formed when the reaction was over. The temperature element of the definition was often omitted.
notes.3cv: M any candidates were aware that large pieces of zinc carbonate have a smaller surface area than powder. However, only a minority of candidates appreciated that an explanation in terms of particles was asked for. This required the decrease in collision frequency of particles (or the equivalent term) to be included in the answer. A decrease in collision frequency alone was insufficient, as was ‘fewer collisions of particles’ without reference to time. Candidates should be reminded that answers describing ‘less chance of collisions’ are not creditworthy. Other commonly seen errors were: changes to particle kinetic energy or speed; fewer particles present.
notes.3cvi: Many answers to this question made vague references to substances containing water but lacked the specific idea of the substance being ‘chemically combined with water’, as given in the syllabus definition.
notes.4ai: Although generally well done, some candidates seemed unaware that the 4 at the beginning of 4 FeS multiplies everything in the formula that follows it by 4 , including the S. Many incorrect answers of 5, 2 and 2 were seen, where the number of O and Fe in the equation would be balanced but not the S. In some cases, crossings out made candidate responses difficult to read.
notes.4aii: This was answered very well. A single covalent bond was drawn occasionally. Some candidates used only one symbol to represent the electrons from both oxygen atoms and did not gain full credit as the resultant is not a ‘dot - and - c ross’ diagram. It is good practice to draw non - bonding electrons in pairs as it is easier to check that atoms have a complete octet and this helps reduce the likelihood of miscounting.
notes.4bi: Candidates should learn the temperatures, pressures and catalysts as given in the syllabus for the Contact process as these are the typical conditions . Units and a suitable value were required for both temperature and pressure. Vanadium( V ) oxide had to be both named and referred to as the catalyst. The first marking point for the temperature was most often achieved. Some candidates gave the pressure and catalyst associated with the Haber process. The oxidation state of vanadium( V ) oxide was often incorrect or it was not referred to as the catalyst.
notes.4bii: This was fairly well answered. Common errors were: correct species but unbalanced equation; the use of O instead of O .
notes.4biii: This was very well answered and only those candidates who did not know the formula for sulfuric acid tended to encounter difficulties.
notes.4c: Oxidation numbers are still proving challenging. Ca ndidates who performed less well often gave the relative atomic or molecular masses rather than the oxidation numbers. The oxidation number of carbon in CO was found to be particularly difficult and a wide variety of incorrect answers was seen. A common near - miss error was the omission of the + sign from + 4. Oxidation numbers written as ionic charges or Roman numerals did not gain credit. Candidates need to be aware that a key part of an oxidation num ber is the positive or negative sign preceding the integer. Integers alone are not oxidation numbers. Candidates should be aware that 4 + is technically incorrect.
notes.4d: Candidates should be reminded that fractions as answers to calculations will not receive credit as the final answer has not been calculated. The number of moles of sodium hydrogencarbonate proved the easiest mark to achieve as most candidates knew that they had to use both the mass of 4.20 g and the given M r of 84. The only common errors seen were multiplying both numbers together or division of 84 by 4.20. Some candidates did not correctly deduce the number of moles of carbon dioxide as they did not make use of the mole ratio of 1 : 1 from the given equation. A common error here was to double or halve the number of moles of sodium hydrogencar bonate.
notes.5a: These were easily obtained recall marks for well - prepared candidates who had learnt the conditions of a reversible reaction at equilibrium given in the syllabus. However, some candidates needed to be more precise with their use of language. Vague statement s such as ‘the forward reaction equals the reverse reaction’ were seen, which has no reference to the rates of both reactions. ‘Concentrations of reactants and products are the same’ was also too ambiguous to gain credit although ‘concentrations of reactan ts and products remain the same’ is acceptable. Other common errors seen were: describing the rates as constant rather than equal; describing the concentrations as equal rather than no longer changing.
notes.5bi: Many candidates knew that a lower temperature would lead to the disadvantage of a decrease in the rate of the reaction. However, some only wrote about lower collision frequency or fewer particles with energy equal to or above the activation energy and this was insufficient without the consequential reduced reaction rate. A reduction in the yield of ethanoic acid was incorrect for an exothermic reaction. Candidates tended to find the second part of the question more challenging and many only wrote about an equilibrium shift without describing the resultant decrease in yield. This was insufficient to gain credit as the disadvantage is the low yield. Some th ought that at a higher temperature the reaction would be too fast, would become dangerous or that enzyme denaturation would occur.
notes.5bii: Most candidates coped well with predicting the effects of changing the reaction conditions. Candidates most commonly knew that a catalyst would not change the concentration of ethanoic acid. The fact that a pressure increase would increase the concentration was less well known.
notes.5biii: Those candidates who correctly suggested cobalt as the catalyst were usually able to give the correct reason. However, many candidates were either unfamiliar with the use of transition elements as catalysts or did not use their Periodic Table to identify c obalt as being a transition element. A variety of reasons for choosing an incorrect element was seen, such as it being very reactive or unreactive.
notes.5ci: Most candidates knew that methanoic acid was the carboxylic acid containing one carbon atom. C andidates who performed less well named ethanoic acid or methane.
notes.5cii: This proved to be one of the most difficult questions on the paper. Many answers were forms of structural formulae, for example C H COOH or were incorrect molecular formulae. Some 3 7 candidates gave both a molecular formula and a structural formula but credit is not awarded when a candidate gives two contradictory answers.
notes.5di: This was a demanding question for many and although most attempts were organic molecules containing two carbon atoms, they often bore no resemblance to an ester. A very common error was drawing the displayed formula of ethanoic acid instead of methyl metha noate, as incorrect placement of the bridging oxygen atom resulted in a carboxyl group rather than an ester linkage.
notes.5dii: Butanoic acid was well known by many candidates as the carboxylic acid reacting. However, very few candidates named propan - 1 - ol as the alcohol because propanol was usually given and this name does not indicate the position of the hydroxyl functional group. Candidates should use the IUPAC name propan - 1 - ol rather than 1 - propanol or the older name of n - propyl alcohol. ( e ) Many candidates seemed well practiced in the determination of empirical formula s from percentage composition and there were some excellent answers to this question in which all steps of the working were clearly shown. However, some candidates had no idea how to proceed and gave final answers that were just large numbers. Common errors included: • dividing all three percentages by the smallest percentage of 9.80 instead of using the A r of each element • dividing the percentages by the atomic numbers instead of the A of each element • incorrectly approximating the number of moles of atoms from 4.90 : 9.80 : 1.96 to 5 : 10 : 1, omitting the step of dividing the number of moles of atoms by the smallest one, 1.96. This method did not achieve full credit • Those who correctly divided all the moles of atoms by the smallest one and achieved the values of 2.5 : 5 : 1 often went on to approximate 2.5 to either 2 or 3 instead of multiplying all the values by 2, resulting in incorrect empirical formulae of either C 2 H 5 O or C 3 H 5 O instead of C H O . 5 10 2
notes.6a: Most candidates knew that Group I elements are known as alkali metals. The only common incorrect answers were alkali (alone) and alkaline metals. Alkaline earth metals was occasionally seen.
notes.6b: This was also very well answered with the only common incorrect answer being francium.
notes.6ci: The most commonly awarded marking point was bubbling. The question asked for two observations but answers were often statements such as ‘a gas is produced’ or ‘hydrogen is given off’ rather than observations. Comments on the rate or violence of the reactio n were ignored. Common incorrect observations given were colour changes of the solution and precipitates. Candidates should be made aware that giving two observations worded in different ways , for example ‘fizzing’ and ‘bubbling’, will only be cred ited once.
notes.6cii: Whilst most candidates knew that hydrogen would be formed, very few realised that the other product would be lithium hydroxide. Lithium oxide was a very common incorrect product.
notes.6d: This question was well answered. The majority of candidates knew that Group I elements have lower density and are less hard than transition elements. Common incorrect properties were: lower melting points/boiling points (given in the question); chemical pr operties instead of physical ones, including formation of colourless compounds; physical properties common to all metals such as malleability.
notes.6ei: The colours and states of the halogens are given in the syllabus and chlorine was expected to be a pale yellow - green gas at r.t.p. Candidates who performed less well often described chlorine as a white solid, probably because of confusion with the silver c hloride precipitate given in the test for chloride ions.
notes.6eii: Candidates found this the most difficult question on the paper. Very few realised that to make the equation ionic they needed to remove the spectator potassium ions, leaving the halide ions and the covalent molecules. Frequently seen incorrect answers wer e: ionic half - equations; equations showing the formation of either KBr or KC l from K and halide ion; charges on the chlorine and bromine molecules; chloride ions as reactants and bromide ions as products. Candidates that performed less well often si mply copied the equation given in the question.
notes.6eiii: In general, candidates were confident in performing the two calculations involving bond energies and the answers 392 kJ and 436 kJ were frequently seen. However, a significant number carried out the final subtraction in reverse to give + 44 kJ / mol.
